title: Search Engine Optimization (SEO): Professional Audits and Client Practice

modules.title: Professional SEO Foundations: Value, Technical Language and Markets
modules.overview: You will learn to size an SEO opportunity from a site's own data, speak the technical language developers expect, and choose between local, multi-country and remote client markets. Every method is grounded in Google's own documentation.

lessons.title: Sizing the search opportunity from a website's own data
objectives: Separate branded from non-branded search demand in Search Console data
Find striking-distance queries where a ranking gain is realistic
Build a simple clicks-to-revenue estimate using only the client's own numbers
Present the estimate as a range, never as a promise

blocks.text: At beginner level, people learn that SEO helps a business "show up on Google". At professional level, a client or employer asks a harder question: **how much is better search visibility worth to us, and where should we start?** This lesson teaches you to answer that question with the website's own data instead of guesses or borrowed industry figures.

blocks.name: growth-analytics
blocks.alt: A woman reviewing a rising analytics chart
blocks.caption: Opportunity sizing turns a site's own search data into a business case before any work begins.

blocks.text: The four numbers that connect search to money

Every search visit passes through the same chain. Google shows a page in results (an **impression**). Some searchers click (**clicks**, and clicks divided by impressions is the **click-through rate** or CTR, as Search Console defines it). Some of those visitors take a valuable action such as an order, a quote request or a booking (**conversions**). Each conversion is worth some amount to the business (**value per conversion**).

blocks.title: From search result to revenue
items: Impressions in Search Console
Clicks (impressions x CTR)
Visits in analytics
Conversions (visits x rate)
Revenue (conversions x value)
blocks.caption: Each step multiplies by a rate you can measure on the client's own site, so the estimate is grounded in their reality.

blocks.text: Impressions, clicks, CTR and average position come from **Google Search Console**, in the Performance report. The conversion rate comes from the client's analytics (for example Google Analytics 4) or, for small businesses, from their own order book or WhatsApp records. Value per conversion comes from the owner: average order value for a shop, or average job value for a service firm.
Step one: split branded and non-branded demand

**Branded queries** contain the business name, for example "Zara Fabrics Lagos". People searching these already know the business, so the site usually ranks first anyway. **Non-branded queries** describe a need, for example "ankara fabric wholesale lagos". These are where SEO creates new customers. In the Performance report, add a query filter that excludes the brand name and its common misspellings, then note total non-branded impressions and clicks. If non-branded clicks are tiny compared with branded clicks, the site is mostly being found by people who already know it, which is itself a key finding for the client.

head: Query type
Example
What it tells you
rows: Reputation and repeat demand; SEO rarely changes it much
"how many yards of ankara for a gown"
Content opportunity; may lead to sales later
Direct sales opportunity; usually the first priority

blocks.text: Step two: find striking-distance queries

A page sitting at average position 8 to 20 for a relevant query is said to be in **striking distance**: Google already considers it relevant, but it is just below the results most people click. Improving that page (its title, its content depth, its internal links) is usually faster than ranking a brand-new page from nothing. Sort the non-branded queries by impressions, then keep the ones with an average position between roughly 8 and 20 and clear commercial intent. Open the Pages tab for each to see which URL is ranking.

blocks.title: Average position is an average
blocks.text: Search Console reports the average of the topmost position your site held each time it appeared. A value of 11.4 can hide days at position 6 and days at position 20. Look at the trend over several weeks before you treat a query as stable.
Step three: use the site's own CTR, not internet averages

You will find many published "CTR by position" charts online. They come from different studies, different countries and different years, and they rarely match a specific site. A more honest method is to look at the client's own queries that already rank in positions 3 to 5 and calculate their average CTR. That becomes your assumption for what a moved query might achieve. Then always build two cases: an optimistic one using that CTR, and a conservative one using half of it.

blocks.title: Worked example: is one query worth the work?
blocks.context: For example, Kemi sells ankara and lace online from Lagos and asks whether SEO is worth paying for. Her Search Console data for the last three months shows the non-branded query "ankara fabric wholesale lagos" with 12,000 impressions, 96 clicks and an average position of 11.4. Her queries that already sit in positions 3 to 5 average a 6% CTR. Her analytics show 1.5% of organic visitors place an order, and her average order is about 45,000 naira (approximate, from her own records).
steps: Optimistic case: 12,000 x 6% = 720 clicks. Extra clicks: 720 - 96 = 624.
Extra orders: 624 x 1.5% = 9.36, about 9 orders in three months.
Extra revenue: 9.36 x 45,000 = 421,200 naira (approximate).
Conservative case: CTR of 3% gives 360 clicks, so 264 extra clicks, 3.96 extra orders and about 178,200 naira over three months.
She records both figures, the assumptions behind them and the date range used.
blocks.result: Kemi now knows this one query could be worth roughly 178,000 to 421,000 naira of extra sales per quarter if the page reaches the top five. That range, not a guarantee, tells her the page deserves attention first.

blocks.text: Presenting the estimate honestly

Google's own guidance on hiring an SEO is direct: no one can guarantee a number one ranking on Google. Your estimate must therefore be labelled as a scenario. Show the inputs, the formula and both cases. Point out what could make it wrong: competitors improving, seasonal demand (fabric sales may peak before festive seasons), or changes to how Google lays out results. Clients trust consultants who show their working.

items: Use a recent, equal-length date range, and say which one.
Exclude branded queries before calculating opportunity.
Use the client's own CTR, conversion rate and order value.
Give a conservative and an optimistic case.
Never add up opportunity from queries that compete for the same page twice.

blocks.title: Save data on your phone
blocks.text: Search Console lets you export the Performance table. Exporting once to Google Sheets and working there uses far less mobile data than reloading the report each time you change a filter.

takeaways: Search value flows through impressions, CTR, conversion rate and value per conversion.
Non-branded queries show where SEO can win new customers.
Striking-distance queries (about positions 8 to 20) are often the fastest wins.
Use the client's own CTR and conversion data and always give a range.

activity.title: Size one opportunity
steps: Open Search Console for a site you can access (your own, a friend's with permission, or a practice site).
Filter out branded queries and export the last three months of query data.
List five non-branded queries with average position between 8 and 20.
Work out the site's own average CTR for queries in positions 3 to 5.
Build an optimistic and a conservative estimate for the best query, showing every calculation.
activity.evidence: A spreadsheet tab with the five queries, the CTR assumption and both estimates with formulas visible.

lessons.title: Technical vocabulary at professional depth: status codes, redirects and canonicals
objectives: Read common HTTP status codes and say what each means for search
Choose between permanent and temporary redirects and avoid chains
Explain how canonical signals consolidate duplicate URLs
Tell the difference between blocking crawling and blocking indexing

blocks.text: Clients and developers judge an SEO professional by how precisely she speaks. Saying "the page is broken" is not enough; saying "the old URL returns a 404 and has 14 internal links pointing to it" gets the problem fixed. This lesson gives you the technical vocabulary you will use in every audit, with Google's own rules behind each term.

blocks.name: code-inspection
blocks.alt: A person inspecting code on a large screen
blocks.caption: Technical SEO starts with reading what the server actually says about each URL.

blocks.text: HTTP status codes

Every time a browser or Googlebot requests a URL, the server answers with a three-digit **status code** before sending any content. You can see it in Search Console's URL Inspection tool, in a crawler such as Screaming Frog, or in your browser's developer tools.

head: Code
Meaning
What it means for SEO
rows: The page can be indexed if nothing else blocks it
Google treats the target as the canonical URL
Google follows it but does not treat it as a canonical signal
Fine for pages that are truly gone; fix internal links to them
A clearer signal that a page was removed on purpose
Google cannot read the page; repeated errors hurt crawling

blocks.text: Redirects: permanent or temporary

Google's documentation separates redirects into two families. **Permanent** redirects (301, 308, and an instant meta refresh) tell Google the new URL should replace the old one in results. **Temporary** redirects (302, 303, 307) are followed, but Google may keep the old URL indexed. Use a permanent redirect when you are sure it will not be reverted, for example after moving a site from http to https. Google also prefers **server-side** redirects; JavaScript redirects only work if Google successfully renders the page.

A **redirect chain** is when URL A redirects to B, which redirects to C. Each extra hop slows visitors and wastes crawling. Search Console reports a "Redirect error" when a chain is too long or loops. The professional fix is to point every old URL straight at the final destination in one hop.
Duplicate URLs and canonicalisation

The same page often lives at several addresses: with and without https, with and without www, and with tracking parameters such as ?utm_source=whatsapp or ?gclid=. Google groups these duplicates and picks one **canonical** URL to show in results. You influence that choice with signals. In Google's own order of strength: a **redirect** is a strong signal, a **rel="canonical"** link in the page head is a strong signal, and listing a URL in the **XML sitemap** is a weak signal. Use them together and make sure they agree.

items: Put a self-referencing canonical tag on every canonical page, with an absolute URL (https://www.example.com/page, not /page).
Link internally to the canonical version only.
List only canonical URLs in the sitemap.
Do not use robots.txt, the URL removal tool or noindex to choose a canonical; Google advises against all three for this purpose.

blocks.title: Worked example: one homepage, five addresses
blocks.context: For example, Halima manages the website of an events company in Kaduna. A crawl shows the homepage answering at http://eventsco.ng, http://www.eventsco.ng, https://eventsco.ng, https://www.eventsco.ng and https://www.eventsco.ng/?utm_source=whatsapp. Search Console marks some as "Duplicate without user-selected canonical".
steps: She chooses https://www.eventsco.ng/ as the canonical, because most backlinks already point there.
She tests each variant and finds http://eventsco.ng goes to https://eventsco.ng, then to https://www.eventsco.ng: a chain of two hops.
She asks the developer for one server-side 301 rule so every http and non-www variant goes straight to https://www.eventsco.ng/ in a single hop.
The UTM version stays live (the WhatsApp campaign needs it) but gets a canonical tag pointing to https://www.eventsco.ng/.
She checks that the sitemap and the site menu use only the canonical URL, then re-tests with URL Inspection.
blocks.result: Four variants now redirect in one hop, the tracking URL consolidates by canonical tag, and all signals agree. Halima logs the change with the date so she can check the Page indexing report two to four weeks later.

blocks.text: Blocking crawling is not blocking indexing

blocks.title: robots.txt Disallow versus noindex
items: robots.txt Disallow
noindex tag or header
left: URL can still be indexed from links
Google cannot see tags on the page
Use to save crawling on endless filters
right: Googlebot must crawl to see it
Keeps the page out of results
Do not also block it in robots.txt
Use for thank-you or internal search pages
blocks.caption: Many sites block a page in robots.txt and add noindex, so Google never sees the noindex: pick the tool that matches the goal.

blocks.text: This confusion appears in many audits. Search Console even has a warning status, "Indexed, though blocked by robots.txt", for pages Google indexed from links without being allowed to crawl them. If the goal is "keep this out of search results", use noindex and let Google crawl the page.
Rendering and structured data in one paragraph each

**Rendering** is Google running a page's JavaScript to see the final content, much as a browser does. If important text, links or canonical tags only appear after scripts run, they may be seen late or not at all. Google recommends putting canonical tags in the HTML source rather than adding them by script. Compare "view source" with the rendered HTML in URL Inspection when you suspect a problem.

**Structured data** is code, usually in JSON-LD format, that labels page content for search engines: an organisation's name and logo, a product's price, an event's date. It can make a page eligible for richer result features, but it is not a promise of them, and it must describe content that visitors can actually see on the page.

blocks.title: Core Web Vitals thresholds
blocks.text: For page experience, web.dev lists good scores as Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds, Interaction to Next Paint of 200 milliseconds or less, and Cumulative Layout Shift of 0.1 or less, measured at the 75th percentile of page loads. INP replaced First Input Delay as a Core Web Vital in 2024.

takeaways: Status codes tell you what the server says before any content loads.
301 and 308 are permanent and consolidate to the target; 302 and 307 do not.
Redirect, canonical tag and sitemap are canonical signals of decreasing strength; make them agree.
robots.txt controls crawling, noindex controls indexing; never combine them on a page you want removed.

activity.title: Map one site's URL variants
steps: Pick a real website and type its homepage with http, https, www and non-www (four combinations).
Note where each lands and how many hops it takes (a free online redirect checker or browser developer tools will show this).
View the page source and find the rel="canonical" tag, if any.
Write which URL should be canonical and the exact fix you would request from a developer.
activity.evidence: A four-row table of variants, hops and final URL, plus a two-sentence fix request.

lessons.title: Global and African markets: local, multi-country and remote client SEO
objectives: Compare three markets for SEO work: local African businesses, multi-country brands and remote international clients
Choose a URL structure for a site that targets several countries
Write correct hreflang annotations with x-default
Adapt SEO advice to mobile-first, data-conscious audiences

blocks.text: SEO work can be delivered from anywhere with a laptop and a connection, so a Nigerian SEO professional competes in three different markets at once. Each needs a different kind of expertise. Knowing which one you are serving shapes your pricing, your technical recommendations and how you find clients.

blocks.name: connected-world
blocks.alt: A globe connected by lines to people in several places
blocks.caption: International SEO is about sending each searcher to the version of a site made for their country and language.

blocks.text: Three markets, three skill sets

head: Market
Typical client
Skills that matter most
rows: A clinic, school, caterer or logistics firm serving one city
Local search, mobile speed on modest phones, simple sites, explaining SEO in plain language
A Lagos skincare brand also selling in Ghana and to the UK diaspora
Country targeting, hreflang, currency and delivery pages, analytics by country
A company abroad hiring through agencies or freelance platforms
Technical audits at scale, clear written reporting, working across time zones

blocks.text: Many people start with local clients, because you can meet them and show results in a familiar market, then add remote work once they have case studies. Whichever you choose, the rest of this course works the same way; only the scale and the stakes change.
Mobile-first and data-conscious audiences

Google uses the mobile version of a site for indexing and ranking, so whatever is missing on mobile is effectively missing for Google. In Nigerian and many other African markets, most visitors browse on smartphones and pay for data by the bundle. Practical consequences: compress images and serve modern formats such as WebP, avoid auto-playing video, keep key text and contact details in the HTML rather than inside images, and test pages on a mid-range Android phone over mobile data, not only on office Wi-Fi.
Choosing a structure for several countries

blocks.title: Country domains versus subfolders
items: Separate country domains
Subfolders on one domain
left: More domains to renew and maintain
right: Needs hreflang to separate countries clearly
blocks.caption: Small and growing brands usually manage subfolders more easily; established brands with local teams sometimes justify separate country domains.

blocks.text: hreflang: telling Google which version is for whom

When pages exist in different languages, or in the same language for different countries, the **hreflang** annotation tells Google which version to show to which searcher. Google accepts it in three equivalent places: link tags in the HTML head, HTTP headers, or the XML sitemap. The rules from Google's documentation that most often catch people out:

items: The code is a language code in ISO 639-1 format, optionally followed by a region code in ISO 3166-1 Alpha 2 format: en-NG, en-GH, en-GB.
A region alone is invalid: "NG" will not work, it must be "en-NG".
"UK" is not a valid region code; the United Kingdom is GB, so use en-GB.
Every version must list itself and all the others. If two pages do not point to each other, the annotations are ignored.
x-default marks the fallback page for searchers who match none of the listed versions, often a country selector or the main international page.

blocks.title: Worked example: hreflang for a skincare brand in three markets
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma's skincare brand sells from Lagos. Her shea body butter has three versions: brand.com/ng/shea-butter (naira prices, Lagos and Abuja delivery), brand.com/gh/shea-butter (cedi prices, Accra delivery) and brand.com/uk/shea-butter (pound prices, UK shipping). She also has brand.com/shea-butter for everyone else.
steps: She maps each URL to a code: /ng/ is en-NG, /gh/ is en-GH, /uk/ is en-GB (not en-UK), and the general page is x-default.
She writes four link tags, for example: <link rel="alternate" hreflang="en-GB" href="https://brand.com/uk/shea-butter" />, one for each version including x-default.
She places the same set of four tags in the head of all four pages, so each page references itself and the other three: 4 pages x 4 tags = 16 tags in total.
She checks that each version has a self-referencing canonical tag, not a canonical pointing to the Nigerian page, because a canonical to another country page would tell Google to drop that version.
She crawls the four URLs with Screaming Frog's free version, which reports missing return links in its hreflang checks.
blocks.result: A searcher in Accra is more likely to see the cedi page and one in London the pound page, and Google no longer treats the three country pages as competing duplicates.

blocks.title: Language codes for local languages
blocks.text: Hausa (ha), Yoruba (yo), Igbo (ig) and Swahili (sw) have two-letter ISO 639-1 codes. Nigerian Pidgin does not have a two-letter ISO 639-1 code, so check Google's current hreflang documentation before tagging Pidgin pages rather than inventing a code.
Translation is not localisation

Machine-translating a page into Yoruba or French and publishing it rarely helps. Real localisation changes prices and currency, delivery and payment options (Paystack, Opay or Moniepoint for Nigerian buyers, for instance), phone formats, examples and the words local people actually search. Do keyword research separately for each market: Ghanaian and Nigerian shoppers may use different words for the same product.
Finding your first focus

Pick one market to start. For local work, list ten businesses in one sector in your city and check whether they appear for their main service plus city name. For multi-country work, look for Nigerian brands already shipping abroad that show prices in only one currency. For remote work, choose one industry you understand well, so your audits read like an insider wrote them.

takeaways: Local, multi-country and remote international clients need different SEO skills.
Mobile-first indexing and costly data make lightweight mobile pages essential in African markets.
hreflang needs valid ISO codes, return links on every version and usually an x-default.
Localisation means currency, delivery, payment and local search terms, not just translation.

activity.title: Choose and test your market
steps: Decide which of the three markets you will focus on first and write one sentence explaining why.
Find one real website in that market that serves more than one country or language, or a local business site.
Check its source code for hreflang tags and note any errors (invalid codes, missing return links, missing x-default).
Load its key page on your phone over mobile data and note anything slow or missing compared with desktop.
activity.evidence: A short note naming your chosen market and listing at least three specific findings from the site you tested.

quiz.q: Kemi's query has 8,000 impressions and 64 clicks at average position 12. Her own top-five queries average 5% CTR. In the optimistic case, how many extra clicks could this query bring?
quiz.explain: 8,000 x 5% = 400 clicks. Subtract the current 64 clicks: 400 - 64 = 336 extra clicks.

quiz.q: Why should she remove branded queries before sizing an SEO opportunity?
options: Branded queries are not counted by Search Console
People searching the brand already find the site, so SEO adds little there
Google penalises sites with branded searches
Branded queries always have zero CTR
quiz.explain: Branded searchers already know the business and the site usually ranks first; new customers come mainly from non-branded queries.

quiz.q: A site moved from http to https for good. Which redirect should the developer use?
options: 301 Moved Permanently, in a single hop
A JavaScript redirect after five seconds
quiz.explain: A permanent server-side redirect such as 301 tells Google the https URL should replace the old one; one hop avoids chains.

quiz.q: A thank-you page must stay out of Google results. What is the correct approach?
options: Add noindex and allow Google to crawl it
Add noindex and also block it in robots.txt
Add it to the XML sitemap
quiz.explain: Google must crawl the page to see noindex. Blocking it in robots.txt hides the noindex, and the URL may still be indexed from links.

quiz.q: Which hreflang value is valid for a page meant for English speakers in the United Kingdom?
quiz.explain: hreflang needs an ISO 639-1 language code plus an optional ISO 3166-1 Alpha 2 region code. The UK's region code is GB, and a region alone is invalid.

quiz.q: Ifeoma's Ghana page has a canonical tag pointing to her Nigeria page. What is the likely effect?
options: Google may drop the Ghana page as a duplicate of the Nigeria page
Ghanaian searchers will see the Ghana page more often
hreflang overrides the canonical, so nothing changes
Google will index both and rank them equally
quiz.explain: A canonical says "this page is a copy of that one". Each country version should have a self-referencing canonical so hreflang can work.

modules.title: Professional Tools, Workflow and Quality Assurance
modules.overview: You will use Search Console, a crawler and testing tools at professional depth, turn findings into a scored plan and developer-ready tickets, and prove whether changes worked. The focus is on evidence you can show a client.

lessons.title: The professional audit toolkit: Search Console in depth, a crawler and testing tools
objectives: Use URL Inspection to compare Google's indexed copy with the live page
Triage the Page indexing report by business importance, not by raw counts
Run a crawl of up to 500 URLs with the free Screaming Frog SEO Spider
Know when field data and lab data disagree in PageSpeed Insights

blocks.text: You may already have Search Console connected to a site. Professional work uses the same tools much more deeply, and adds a crawler that sees the site the way Googlebot does. This lesson walks through the five tools that cover most audits, all free, and shows how to read their output without panicking at big numbers.

blocks.name: data-reports
blocks.alt: A woman reviewing several data reports on a board
blocks.caption: An audit combines Google's view of the site with your own crawl of it.

blocks.text: The core toolkit

head: Tool
What it shows
Use it for
rows: How Google crawls, indexes and shows the site
Indexing problems, queries, Core Web Vitals field data
Your own crawl of up to 500 URLs; runs on Windows, macOS and Linux
Broken links, redirects, titles, headings, canonicals, hreflang
Field data from real Chrome users plus a Lighthouse lab test
Speed problems and their likely causes
Rich Results Test and Schema Markup Validator
Checking JSON-LD before and after changes
A second opinion and Bing visibility

blocks.text: URL Inspection: the single most useful check

Paste any URL from the property into the inspection bar at the top of Search Console. You see whether the URL is on Google, which canonical Google selected, whether it was crawled as a smartphone, and the last crawl date. **Test live URL** fetches the page now, so you can compare the live version with what Google has stored. Use **View crawled page** to see the HTML Google rendered; if your main text or links are missing there, rendering is the problem.
The Page indexing report: triage, do not panic

This report groups every known URL into indexed and not indexed, with a reason for each. Large "not indexed" numbers frighten clients, but many reasons are normal. Google's help pages say, for example, that "Page with redirect" and "Alternate page with proper canonical tag" usually need no action, and "Crawled, currently not indexed" and "Discovered, currently not indexed" may resolve on their own. Your job is to ask one question of each reason: **does this group contain pages the business needs in search?**

blocks.title: Triage one indexing reason
items: Open the reason
Export example URLs
Any business-critical pages?
Find the cause
Fix, then Validate fix
blocks.caption: Only reasons that hide important pages become audit findings; the rest are recorded as expected.

blocks.title: Worked example: triaging 1,240 not-indexed URLs
blocks.context: For example, Funmi audits an online bookshop in Ibadan. The Page indexing report shows 1,240 URLs not indexed: 610 Page with redirect, 380 Alternate page with proper canonical tag, 150 Crawled, currently not indexed, 70 Not found (404) and 30 marked noindex. She checks the total: 610 + 380 + 150 + 70 + 30 = 1,240.
steps: Page with redirect (610): example URLs are old http addresses that now redirect to https. Expected, no action.
Alternate with proper canonical (380): sorting and filter URLs such as ?sort=price that point to the main category. Expected, no action.
Crawled, currently not indexed (150): she exports them and finds 22 are real book pages with only a title and price, no description. Finding: thin product pages.
Not found (70): her crawl shows 9 of these are still linked from the site menu and blog. Finding: broken internal links.
noindex (30): 28 are cart and account pages, which is correct, but 2 are the "Nigerian authors" and "School textbooks" categories. Finding: two money pages wrongly set to noindex.
blocks.result: Of 1,240 URLs, only 22 + 9 + 2 = 33 need action, and the two noindexed categories are the most urgent. Funmi reports three clear findings instead of a frightening number.

blocks.text: Running a crawl with Screaming Frog

items: Install the SEO Spider on a laptop (it does not run on phones).
Enter the homepage URL and start the crawl; the free version stops at 500 URLs, enough for most small business sites.
Open the Response Codes tab and filter Client Error (4xx); for each broken URL, use the Inlinks tab at the bottom to see which pages link to it.
Check Page Titles and Meta Description tabs for missing, duplicate, too long or too short entries.
Check the Canonicals and Directives tabs for pages that are canonicalised elsewhere or noindexed by mistake.
Export the tabs you need to a spreadsheet and record the crawl date.

blocks.title: Crawl politely
blocks.text: A crawler can send many requests quickly. On small shared hosting, lower the crawl speed in the configuration so you do not slow the client's site for real customers, and always crawl only sites you have permission to audit.
Field data and lab data

PageSpeed Insights shows two kinds of results. **Field data** comes from real Chrome users over the previous 28 days and is what the Core Web Vitals assessment uses, judged at the 75th percentile. **Lab data** is a single Lighthouse test from Google's servers under set conditions. They often disagree. If field data is good but lab data is poor, real visitors are fine and the lab test is simply harsher; if field data is poor, real customers are suffering and it belongs in the audit. Small sites may have no field data at all, because not enough Chrome users visited; then you rely on lab data and on testing with a real phone.
Structured data and Bing

Run key templates (homepage, a product or service page, an article) through the Rich Results Test to see which result features the page is eligible for, and through the Schema Markup Validator to check the schema itself. Finally, add the site to Bing Webmaster Tools, which can import properties directly from Search Console. Bing powers results in some other services too, and its site scan is a useful second check.

blocks.title: Request indexing sparingly
blocks.text: The Request indexing button in URL Inspection is useful after fixing an important page. It is not a ranking tool, and pressing it repeatedly does not speed anything up.

takeaways: URL Inspection shows Google's stored version, its chosen canonical and a live test.
Triage indexing reasons by asking whether important pages are affected.
The free Screaming Frog crawls 500 URLs and finds broken links, redirects, titles and canonicals.
Field data reflects real users; lab data is a controlled test. Report field problems first.

activity.title: Run a mini technical check
steps: Inspect your site's homepage and one inner page with URL Inspection and note the Google-selected canonical for each.
Open the Page indexing report and list every not-indexed reason with its count.
For the two largest reasons, export five example URLs and decide whether action is needed.
Run PageSpeed Insights on the homepage and record whether field data exists and the LCP, INP and CLS values.
activity.evidence: A one-page sheet: inspection results, the reason table with your decision for each, and the PageSpeed figures.

lessons.title: From brief to delivery: audit sequence, prioritisation scoring and developer tickets
objectives: Follow a repeatable eight-stage SEO engagement workflow
Score audit findings with Impact x Confidence x Ease
Write implementation tickets a developer can complete without asking questions
Spot critical blockers that must be fixed before anything else

blocks.text: Amateurs hand a client a long list of everything imperfect. Professionals hand over a short, ordered plan where the first items clearly matter most. The difference is a consistent workflow and a scoring method you can explain. This lesson gives you both.

blocks.name: checklist
blocks.alt: A woman ticking items on a large checklist
blocks.caption: A repeatable workflow keeps every engagement consistent, from the first call to the final report.

blocks.text: The engagement workflow

blocks.title: An SEO engagement, start to finish
items: Brief and access
Baseline snapshot
Crawl and audit
Score and prioritise
Tickets and implementation
Verify and report
blocks.caption: Taking a baseline before any change is what lets you prove results later.

items: **Brief and access:** agree goals and get Search Console, analytics and CMS access at the right permission level (Module 3 covers this).
**Baseline snapshot:** export three to sixteen months of Search Console data, organic conversions from analytics, and a full crawl, all dated.
**Crawl and audit:** work through indexing, technical, on-page, content and links in that order, because a site Google cannot index gets nothing from better titles.
**Score and prioritise:** give every finding the same score (below).
**Tickets and implementation:** turn top findings into tickets for the developer, writer or owner.
**Verify and report:** confirm each fix is live and measure it (next lesson).

blocks.text: Critical blockers come first

Some issues stop a site from appearing in search at all. Check for these before scoring anything else: a sitewide noindex left over from development, a robots.txt line "Disallow: /" blocking everything, canonical tags pointing to a staging or old domain, the whole site returning server errors, or the https version redirecting back to http. These go to the top of the list with the label **critical** and are reported to the client the same day.

blocks.title: The staging leftover
blocks.text: When developers copy a site from a test server, settings such as noindex or canonicals to the test domain sometimes come with it. After any site launch or redesign, check the homepage source and URL Inspection immediately.
Scoring with Impact x Confidence x Ease

Give each finding three scores from 1 to 5. **Impact**: how much it could change visibility or conversions for pages the business cares about. **Confidence**: how sure you are, based on evidence, that fixing it will help. **Ease**: how easy it is to implement (5 is very easy). Multiply them. The maximum is 5 x 5 x 5 = 125. The score is not science; its value is that it makes your reasoning visible and consistent, and the client can challenge a single number instead of the whole plan.

blocks.title: Worked example: ordering six findings
blocks.context: For example, Ada audits the website of a tour company in Calabar. She has six findings and scores each one.
steps: A. Homepage canonical points to the old staging domain: Impact 5, Confidence 5, Ease 5 = 125.
B. 38 tour pages share one identical title: 4 x 4 x 3 = 48.
F. 14 internal links point to 404 pages: 2 x 5 x 4 = 40.
D. 60 thin blog tag pages are indexed: 2 x 3 x 4 = 24.
C. Mobile LCP is 4.8 seconds on tour pages, above the 4-second poor threshold: 3 x 3 x 2 = 18.
E. No Organization structured data: 1 x 3 x 5 = 15.
blocks.result: Her order is A (125, also a critical blocker), B (48), F (40), D (24), C (18), E (15). The slow pages matter, but they need a developer and more time, so they come after quicker, high-confidence fixes.

head: Score range
Label
Typical action
rows: Report same day, fix this week

blocks.text: Writing tickets a developer can act on

A finding in a report explains a problem. A **ticket** tells one person exactly what to do and how everyone will know it is done. Many small businesses use a WhatsApp group or a shared Google Sheet instead of formal ticket software; the content matters more than the tool. Each ticket needs:

items: A short title naming the change, for example "Fix homepage canonical to live domain".
The affected URLs or template (attach the exported list rather than describing it).
The current state and the required state, written precisely.
Acceptance criteria: the exact check that proves it is done.
Priority and owner.

blocks.title: Worked example: Ada's ticket for finding B
blocks.context: Ada writes the ticket for the 38 duplicate tour titles. The tour pages are built from one WordPress template.
steps: Title: Unique title tags for all tour pages.
Current: all 38 tour pages use the title "Tours | Calabar Tours".

Required: each title follows the pattern "[Tour name], [duration] | Calabar Tours", for example "Obudu Mountain Resort Trip, 2 Days | Calabar Tours". The attached sheet lists all 38 new titles, each written by Ada.
Acceptance: a fresh Screaming Frog crawl shows zero duplicate titles among tour URLs, and three randomly chosen pages show the new title in view source.
Priority: High. Owner: the site developer, with Ada checking.
blocks.result: The developer can finish the job without a meeting, and Ada can confirm it in ten minutes.

blocks.text: Notice that Ada wrote the 38 titles herself. Do the thinking work in the ticket; developers are not copywriters, and vague tickets such as "improve titles" are the most common reason SEO recommendations never get implemented.

takeaways: Follow the same workflow every time, and take a dated baseline before changing anything.
Critical blockers such as stray noindex or wrong canonicals go first, whatever their score.
Impact x Confidence x Ease makes prioritisation visible and easy to discuss.
Good tickets state current state, required state, acceptance criteria and owner.

activity.title: Score and ticket your findings
steps: List at least five findings from the site you checked in the previous lesson.
Check each for critical blockers first and label any you find.
Score the rest with Impact x Confidence x Ease and sort them.
Write a full ticket, with acceptance criteria, for your top non-critical finding.
activity.evidence: A scored, sorted findings sheet and one complete ticket.

lessons.title: Quality assurance: verifying fixes, measuring change honestly and keeping a change log
objectives: Confirm a fix is live using source code, a recrawl and URL Inspection
Measure a change with equal before-and-after periods and a comparison group
Rule out seasonality and Google updates before claiming credit
Keep a dated change log that supports every claim in your reports

blocks.text: A recommendation is not a result. Between your ticket and a real improvement, many things can go wrong: a fix applied to one page instead of the template, a cache that still serves the old version, or a traffic rise that was really a seasonal spike. Quality assurance protects the client and your reputation.

blocks.name: verify-data
blocks.alt: A person checking data with a magnifying glass and tick marks
blocks.caption: Verify that each change is live before you measure whether it worked.

blocks.text: Three checks that a fix is live

items: **Source check:** open view source on two or three affected pages and confirm the exact change, for example the new title or the corrected canonical. Check on a phone too, because some sites serve different HTML to mobile.
**Recrawl:** run the same crawler settings as your baseline and compare counts: duplicate titles, broken links or noindex pages should have fallen to the expected number.

**Google's view:** use URL Inspection with Test live URL on key pages. For issues listed in the Page indexing report, click Validate fix. Google's help pages say validation typically takes up to about two weeks and will email you as it progresses.

blocks.title: Caching can fool you
blocks.text: Many WordPress sites use caching plugins or a service such as Cloudflare. If the change does not show, ask the developer to clear the cache before you report the fix as failed.
Measuring change honestly

When the fix is live, wait long enough for Google to recrawl and for data to build up, often several weeks for small sites. Then compare **equal-length periods** with the same mix of weekdays: for example 28 days before the change against 28 days after, skipping the first days while Google was still recrawling. Search Console's Performance report can compare two date ranges directly.
Next, look for things other than your change that could explain the difference:

items: **Seasonality:** compare with the same period last year if data exists. School-related searches, festive shopping and rainy-season services all rise and fall.
**Google updates:** check the Google Search Status Dashboard for ranking updates announced during your window.
**Other site changes:** ask whether prices, products, ads or social campaigns changed.
**A comparison group:** pick similar pages you did not change and see how they moved over the same dates.

blocks.title: The QA cycle for every change
items: Make the change
Verify it is live
Wait for recrawl
Measure with comparison
Record in change log
blocks.caption: Each loop ends in the change log, so the next report rests on recorded facts.

blocks.title: Worked example: did the new titles work?
blocks.context: For example, Chioma rewrote titles and meta descriptions on 8 recipe pages of a Nigerian food blog. She compared 28 days before with 28 days after, leaving out the week of the change. She kept 10 similar recipe pages unchanged as a comparison group.
steps: Before: 18,400 impressions, 331 clicks. CTR = 331 / 18,400 = 1.80%. Average position 6.2.
After: 19,100 impressions, 516 clicks. CTR = 516 / 19,100 = 2.70%. Average position 6.0.
Relative CTR change: 2.70 / 1.80 is about 1.50, so CTR rose by about 50%.
Comparison group CTR moved from 2.1% to 2.2%, a relative rise of about 4.8%.
Position barely moved (6.2 to 6.0), and the Status Dashboard showed no announced update in either window.
blocks.result: Because position was stable and the untouched pages hardly changed, the CTR jump is most likely due to the new titles. Chioma reports it as "strong evidence", not proof, and plans to recheck after another 28 days.

blocks.text: The change log

Two cautions about the arithmetic. First, distinguish **percentage points** from **percent**: a CTR moving from 1.80% to 2.70% is a rise of 0.9 percentage points, which is a relative rise of about 50%. Say which one you mean, because clients often confuse them. Second, small numbers swing wildly. A page going from 4 clicks to 8 clicks has "doubled", but that difference could easily be chance, so group similar pages together before drawing conclusions.

A change log is a simple sheet where every SEO-relevant change is recorded on the day it happens. It is the memory of the project, and it lets anyone explain a traffic change months later. Keep it shared with the client.
Staying current without chasing rumours

Search changes constantly, and social media is full of confident claims about secret ranking factors. Base your work on Google Search Central documentation, Search Console help pages and announcements on the Status Dashboard, and treat other sources as ideas to test. Google's own guidance says no one can guarantee a number one ranking on Google, and that a good SEO should be able to tell you what results to expect and in what timeframe. Your QA records are what let you answer that question honestly.

takeaways: Verify every fix three ways: source, recrawl and Google's own tools.
Compare equal periods, skip the recrawl week and use a comparison group.
Check seasonality, Google updates and other site changes before claiming credit.
A shared change log turns your reports into evidence.

activity.title: Start a change log and measure one change
steps: Create a change log sheet with the seven columns from the lesson.
Record one change you make (or made) to a page you control, with the date.
After at least 28 days, compare 28 days before and after in Search Console, excluding the change week.
Choose two unchanged similar pages as a comparison group and calculate CTR for both periods.
activity.evidence: The change log with at least one complete row and a short calculation of before, after and comparison CTR.

quiz.q: The Page indexing report shows 400 URLs as "Alternate page with proper canonical tag". What should Funmi do first?
options: Check examples; this status usually needs no action
quiz.explain: Google says alternate pages with a proper canonical normally need no action. Check examples to confirm they really are duplicates.

quiz.q: A finding scores Impact 4, Confidence 3, Ease 5. What is its score and label using the lesson's bands?
quiz.explain: 4 x 3 x 5 = 60, which falls in the 60 to 125 High band.

quiz.q: After a redesign, the homepage source shows <meta name="robots" content="noindex">. How should this be handled?
options: Score it and put it in the 90-day backlog
Treat it as a critical blocker and report it the same day
Ignore it because the sitemap lists the homepage
Wait two weeks to see if Google ignores it
quiz.explain: A noindex on key pages removes them from search. Critical blockers go first, whatever their score.

quiz.q: Which ticket is most likely to be implemented correctly?
options: "Replace titles on 38 tour pages with the attached list; done when a crawl shows zero duplicates"
"Make the site rank better on Google"
quiz.explain: A good ticket gives the exact change, the URLs and a clear acceptance check.

quiz.q: Before: 10,000 impressions and 150 clicks. After: 10,000 impressions and 210 clicks, with position unchanged. What was the relative CTR change?
quiz.explain: CTR moved from 1.5% to 2.1%. 2.1 / 1.5 = 1.4, a 40% relative rise (0.6 percentage points).

quiz.q: Traffic rose after Chioma's change, but the same weeks last year also rose sharply. What is the most honest conclusion?
options: The change caused all of the rise
Seasonality may explain some or all of the rise; check a comparison group
Seasonality only matters for paid ads
quiz.explain: A rise that also happened last year may be seasonal. A comparison group of unchanged pages helps separate the two.

modules.title: Consulting Practice: Discovery, Pricing, Reporting and Growth
modules.overview: You will run a discovery call with safe access, price and scope SEO services transparently, write a report an owner understands in minutes, and plan how to win your first clients. This module turns your technical skill into paid, trusted work.

lessons.title: Client discovery: the right questions, safe access and a written brief
objectives: Run a discovery call that uncovers goals, customers, history and constraints
Request Search Console and analytics access at the right permission level
Handle client data in line with the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023
Turn discovery notes into a one-page brief with a measurable goal

blocks.text: Discovery is where SEO projects succeed or fail. If you do not know which enquiries actually make the client money, you will optimise the wrong pages. Google's own advice to business owners hiring an SEO suggests they ask whether the SEO is interested in understanding their business, competitors and customers. Your discovery call is where you show that you are.

blocks.name: business-call
blocks.alt: Two people on a business video call
blocks.caption: A structured discovery call gives you the facts that shape every later recommendation.

blocks.text: Five areas every discovery call covers

blocks.title: Discovery call checklist
items: Business goals and money pages
Target customers and their words
History: past SEO, migrations, penalties
Competitors they actually lose to
Constraints: budget, developer, deadlines
blocks.caption: Cover all five before you promise any deliverable.

items: **Goals:** What does a good month look like? Which services or products bring the most profit? How do enquiries arrive: website form, phone, WhatsApp, walk-in?
**Customers:** Who buys? What words do they use when they call? Ask for five recent enquiries (with personal details removed) and note their phrasing.
**History:** Has anyone done SEO before? Was the site redesigned, moved to a new domain or rebuilt recently? Has traffic ever dropped suddenly?
**Competitors:** Who do they lose jobs to? Then search the main services yourself on a phone and note who actually ranks, which may be different.
**Constraints:** Monthly budget, who can edit the website and how many hours they have, and any dates such as a product launch or a busy season.

blocks.title: Ask about tracking early
blocks.text: Many small businesses cannot say how many enquiries came from Google. Ask how they record enquiries now. If the answer is "we don't", setting up a simple record (a form notification, a phone log or a "how did you find us" question) becomes part of the first month's work.
Getting access the safe way

Never ask a client for their Google password. Search Console and Google Analytics both let owners add other people with their own Google accounts. In Search Console, an owner adds you under Settings, then Users and permissions. Google defines three levels: **owners** can manage users and settings, **full users** can view all data and take most actions, and **restricted users** have limited viewing. For most audits, ask for **full user**. Ownership should stay with the client, so they never lose control of their own property if you stop working together.

head: Access needed
Ask for
Why
rows: Full user on the client's property
See all data and validate fixes without controlling users
Read conversions and traffic without changing settings
A named account for you, not a shared login
Changes are traceable and your access can be removed
Manager, if local SEO is in scope
Edit the profile without owning it

blocks.text: At the end of a project, remind the client to remove your access, or remove yourself. Google warns that a removed verified owner can re-verify unless their verification tokens are also removed, which is one more reason not to become an owner in the first place.

blocks.title: Personal data is the client's responsibility and yours
blocks.text: Analytics, contact forms and CRM exports can contain names, phone numbers and emails. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 governs how personal data is processed in Nigeria. Only request the data you need, prefer aggregated reports over customer lists, keep files in a password-protected account with two-step verification, and delete copies when the project ends.

blocks.title: Worked example: discovery with a logistics company
blocks.context: For example, Blessing is operations manager at a haulage and logistics firm in Port Harcourt. She says the website "brings nothing" and wants SEO.
steps: Goals: most profit comes from contract haulage for companies, not one-off deliveries. Enquiries arrive by phone and WhatsApp, and the office has started noting the source; it recorded 6 enquiries from the website last month.
Customers: procurement officers. Recent enquiries mention "haulage company in Port Harcourt", "truck hire for equipment" and "logistics company Trans Amadi" (an industrial area of the city).
History: the site was rebuilt last year and moved from a .com to a .com.ng domain. Nobody set up redirects. This becomes the first technical question to investigate.
Competitors: Blessing names two firms. A phone search shows a directory site and one of the named firms ranking above them.
Constraints: a freelance developer gives 4 hours a month; budget is fixed for six months.
blocks.result: The written brief says: goal, more qualified contract enquiries from organic search, measured monthly from the office's own enquiry log, starting from 6. First investigation: the unredirected domain move. Access: full user in Search Console, Viewer in GA4, a named WordPress editor account.

blocks.text: The one-page brief

Send the brief to the client within two working days and ask them to confirm it in writing, even by email or WhatsApp reply. Include: business goal, the measurable indicator and its starting value, target customers and their main search phrases, key competitors, known history, constraints, access granted, and what you will deliver next. This page is the anchor for the proposal in the next lesson, and the first thing you reread if the project drifts.

takeaways: Discovery covers goals, customers, history, competitors and constraints.
Ask for full user access in Search Console; ownership stays with the client.
Request only the personal data you need and protect it, in line with the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023.
Confirm a one-page brief in writing before you price anything.

activity.title: Run a practice discovery
steps: Choose a real small business (a friend's or family business is fine) and agree a 20-minute call.
Ask questions from all five discovery areas and take notes.
Search their two main services on your phone and record who ranks in the top five.
Write and send a one-page brief and ask them to confirm it.
activity.evidence: The brief, plus their written confirmation (a screenshot of the reply is enough).

lessons.title: Pricing, proposals and scope control for SEO services
objectives: Compare fixed-fee audits, monthly retainers and project pricing
Build a price from an hours estimate, a rate and a contingency
Write a proposal with clear inclusions, exclusions and client responsibilities
Handle extra requests with a written change request

blocks.text: Underpricing is the most common mistake new SEO consultants make, closely followed by unclear scope. Both lead to the same place: you work far more hours than you are paid for. This lesson shows a transparent way to price SEO work and a proposal structure that protects you and the client.

blocks.name: business-deal
blocks.alt: Two people shaking hands over a signed agreement
blocks.caption: A clear proposal is the start of a fair working relationship, not just a price.

blocks.text: Three pricing models

blocks.title: Fixed audit versus monthly retainer
items: Fixed-fee audit
Monthly retainer
left: Good first engagement with a new client
right: Set hours or tasks every month
blocks.caption: Many consultants start with a fixed audit, then offer a retainer to implement the roadmap it produces.

blocks.text: A third model is **project pricing** for a defined job such as a site migration or a hreflang setup. Whichever model you use, base the price on an honest estimate of hours. Hours are not shown to every client, but they keep you profitable.
Building the price

Your hourly rate depends on your experience, your market and your proof of results; there is no official rate. Research what people with similar experience charge in your target market, then decide. The figures below are illustrative only, to show the arithmetic.

head: Audit task (40-page site)
Hours
rows: On-page and content review of key pages
Writing the report and scored roadmap

blocks.title: Worked example: pricing an audit and a retainer
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi is quoting an online bookshop in Ibadan. She has decided on an illustrative rate of 10,000 naira per hour (approximate, her own choice for this example).
steps: Audit hours from the table: 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 5 + 1 = 20 hours.
Base price: 20 x 10,000 = 200,000 naira.
She adds 15% contingency for surprises such as a messy domain history: 200,000 x 1.15 = 230,000 naira.
For implementation afterwards she proposes a retainer of 16 hours a month: 16 x 10,000 = 160,000 naira per month, with a 3-month minimum: 3 x 160,000 = 480,000 naira.
For a separate remote client abroad she quotes the same 20-hour audit at an illustrative 25 US dollars per hour: 20 x 25 = 500 dollars.
Payment terms: 50% before work starts and 50% on delivery of the report, invoiced through a payment service the client can use, such as Paystack for Nigerian clients.
blocks.result: Every number in Ngozi's proposal traces back to hours and a rate she chose, so she can explain it calmly if the client asks for a discount, and reduce scope rather than simply cutting the price.

blocks.text: What a proposal contains

items: **Summary of their goal** in their words, taken from the confirmed brief.
**Deliverables** with dates, for example "Audit report and scored 90-day roadmap, delivered by 30 June; 60-minute presentation call".
**Inclusions:** the pages, templates or number of URLs covered.
**Exclusions:** what is not included, such as writing new content, link building, paid ads, or development work.
**Client responsibilities:** access within three working days, a named contact, and developer time for fixes.
**Price, payment terms and validity** (for example, valid for 30 days).
**What results to expect:** realistic, with no ranking guarantee, and the indicator you will report on.
**Change requests and ending the agreement:** how extra work is priced and how either side can end a retainer with notice.

blocks.title: Never sell guarantees or shortcuts
blocks.text: Do not promise positions ("page one in 30 days") and do not include purchased links or automated content in a package. Google's spam policies prohibit buying links to manipulate rankings and mass-producing low-value pages, and the client's site, not yours, carries the risk.
Controlling scope during the work

Scope creep usually arrives politely: "While you're in there, could you also rewrite the About page?" Answer warmly and in writing. Confirm the request is outside the agreed scope, give its estimated hours and cost, and ask whether to add it now, swap it for something in the current scope, or leave it for later. Record the decision. A short change request like this, sent on WhatsApp or email, keeps the relationship friendly and your hours paid.

blocks.title: Write the swap option
blocks.text: Offering to swap a new request for an existing task of similar size helps clients with fixed budgets say yes without feeling pressured to spend more.
A change request in practice

Suppose the bookshop owner asks Ngozi to also review 15 blog posts during the audit. Ngozi estimates 15 minutes per post, so 15 x 15 = 225 minutes, about 4 hours. Her message reads: "Happy to help with the blog posts. They are outside the audit scope we agreed. Reviewing all 15 would take about 4 hours, which is 40,000 naira at our agreed rate. We can add it now, swap it for the presentation call and a shorter written walkthrough, or schedule it for the first retainer month. Which would you prefer?" The owner chooses the retainer month, and Ngozi records the decision in the project notes. Nobody feels cheated, and the audit still arrives on time.

Protect your cash flow in the same written way. Send invoices with a clear due date, start work only after the agreed first payment arrives, and pause extra work, politely, when an invoice is overdue. For retainers, invoice at the start of each month, not the end.

takeaways: Fixed audits suit first engagements; retainers suit ongoing implementation.
Price from hours x rate plus contingency, so every figure is explainable.
Proposals list inclusions, exclusions, client duties, payment terms and realistic expectations.
Handle extra requests with a written change request: add, swap or defer.

activity.title: Price and propose
steps: Estimate hours for an audit of the site you used in your discovery practice, task by task.
Choose your hourly rate after researching your market and write down why.
Calculate the audit price with 15% contingency and a 3-month retainer option.
Write a one-page proposal using the eight-part structure.
activity.evidence: Your hours table, calculations and one-page proposal.

lessons.title: The client-ready report, a portfolio case study and your 90-day outreach plan
objectives: Structure an audit report so an owner understands it in five minutes
Translate technical findings into business impact
Turn a project into an honest, permission-based case study
Build a 90-day outreach plan with funnel targets you can track

blocks.text: Your audit can be technically perfect and still fail if the owner cannot understand it. A business owner reads for three things: what is wrong, what it costs them, and what happens next. This final lesson shows how to write for that reader, turn your work into proof for future clients, and plan your first 90 days of finding them.

blocks.name: report
blocks.alt: A woman presenting a report with charts
blocks.caption: A client-ready report leads with business impact and keeps the technical detail in the appendix.

blocks.text: Report structure

items: **One-page executive summary:** the goal, the three most important findings, the expected direction of results and the first three actions.
**Findings in priority order:** each with what you found, why it matters for the business, the evidence, and the recommended fix.
**Roadmap:** the scored list grouped into days 1 to 30, 31 to 60 and 61 to 90, with owners.
**Measurement plan:** the indicator from the brief, its starting value and when you will report.
**Appendix:** crawl exports, screenshots and technical details for the developer.

blocks.text: From jargon to business impact

head: Technical finding
Plain-language version for the owner
rows: 212 product URLs: Duplicate without user-selected canonical
Google sees 212 near-copies of your product pages and may show the wrong version, such as one with a tracking code
Old .com domain returns 404s instead of 301 redirects
Visitors and Google following old links to your previous website hit dead pages, so the value of those links is lost
Mobile LCP 4.8 s (poor) on service pages
On a typical phone, your main service pages take almost five seconds to show their main content
Two category pages set to noindex
Your two best-selling categories are hidden from Google completely

blocks.text: Notice that the plain versions keep the numbers. Owners trust specific facts. Remove the jargon, not the evidence. Where you can, link each finding to the money pages and the indicator from the brief.

blocks.title: Worked example: an executive summary in five sentences
blocks.context: For example, after the discovery with Blessing's Port Harcourt logistics firm, the audit is finished and the owner wants a summary he can read on his phone.
steps: Goal: "You want more contract haulage enquiries from Google; last month the office logged 6 from the website."
Finding 1: "When the site moved to the .com.ng domain, the old addresses were not redirected, so links built over several years now lead to dead pages."
Finding 2: "Your haulage and truck hire pages use the same title, so Google struggles to tell which page answers which search."
Finding 3: "The main service pages take almost five seconds to show content on a phone."
Next steps: "In the first 30 days your developer adds redirects (about 3 of his 4 monthly hours) and I supply new titles; we review the enquiry log at day 60 and day 90."
blocks.result: The owner understands the problem, the cost and the plan without opening the appendix, and the developer has everything he needs inside it.

blocks.text: Building a case study the right way

Your portfolio is evidence. A good case study shows the situation, what you found, what was changed, and what happened, with dates and screenshots. Ask the client's written permission before naming them; if they decline, anonymise it ("a logistics company in Port Harcourt") and blur identifying data in screenshots. Report results honestly, including the time period, and do not crop charts to exaggerate. If results are still early, say so, and present the audit and roadmap as the work sample.

blocks.title: Outreach must respect people
blocks.text: Do not send bulk unsolicited messages, scrape personal numbers or add people to WhatsApp groups without consent. Google itself warns business owners to be wary of SEO firms that send unsolicited email. Contact businesses through their published business channels, personalise every message and stop if asked.
Your 90-day outreach plan

blocks.title: Ninety days from skills to first clients
items: Weeks 1 to 2: niche and offer
Weeks 3 to 4: case study ready
Weeks 5 to 10: personalised outreach
Weeks 11 to 13: review and adjust
blocks.caption: Outreach starts only once you have one piece of proof to show.

blocks.text: Choose one niche you can describe in a sentence, for example "private schools in Abuja" or "Nigerian fashion brands shipping to the UK". Prepare one offer, such as a fixed-fee audit. Then plan outreach with targets you set yourself and later replace with your real results.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning the funnel
blocks.context: For example, Zainab targets logistics and haulage firms in Rivers State. She uses her own planning assumptions, not industry figures, and will update them after the first month.
steps: She plans to contact 80 businesses over weeks 5 to 10, about 13 or 14 a week, each with a personal note naming one specific issue she saw on their site.
Assumed reply rate 15%: 80 x 15% = 12 replies.
Assumed half of replies book a call: 12 / 2 = 6 discovery calls.
Assumed one in three calls accepts a proposal: 6 / 3 = 2 new clients.
At week 8 she compares her real numbers with the plan and changes the message or the niche if replies are far below 12.
blocks.result: Zainab has a weekly target she controls (messages sent) and clear checkpoints, rather than waiting and hoping clients appear.

takeaways: Lead every report with a one-page summary an owner can read on a phone.
Translate jargon into business impact but keep the numbers.
Case studies need written permission or anonymisation and honest dates.
Plan outreach with your own assumptions, track weekly and adjust at checkpoints.

activity.title: Write your summary and plan
steps: Write a five-sentence executive summary for the site you have worked on in this course.
Rewrite three technical findings in plain language, keeping the numbers.
Choose your niche and write your offer in two sentences.
Fill in a 90-day funnel plan with your own assumed rates and weekly targets.
activity.evidence: The executive summary, the three translated findings and your funnel plan.

quiz.q: A new client offers to send you their Google account password so you can see Search Console. What should you do?
options: Ask them to add your own Google account as a full user
Ask to be made the only verified owner
Use the password, then change it
quiz.explain: Never use a client's password. Owners can add you as a full user, which gives the data you need while they keep control.

quiz.q: During discovery you learn the site moved to a new domain last year with no redirects. What is the best next step?
options: Ignore it, it was last year
Make it a priority technical investigation in the brief
quiz.explain: An unredirected domain move can lose the value of old links and pages. It belongs at the top of the investigation.

quiz.q: An audit is estimated at 24 hours at an illustrative 8,000 naira per hour, plus 15% contingency. What is the price?
Mid-project, a client asks you to also write five new service pages. What is the professional response?
options: Do it free to keep them happy
Send a change request with hours and cost, offering to add, swap or defer
Do it but rush the agreed work
quiz.explain: A written change request keeps scope clear and gives the client real choices.

quiz.q: Which line belongs in an executive summary for a business owner?
options: "Your two best-selling categories are hidden from Google completely"
"See appendix C for status code exports"
quiz.explain: Owners need plain-language business impact. Technical detail belongs in the appendix.

quiz.q: Zainab plans 60 messages, assumes 20% reply and that half of replies book a call. How many calls does she plan for?

finalQuiz.q: Which set of numbers lets you estimate the revenue value of improving a query's ranking?
options: Impressions, a realistic CTR, conversion rate and value per conversion
Domain age, word count and keyword density
Number of social media followers and likes
finalQuiz.explain: Impressions x CTR gives clicks; clicks x conversion rate gives conversions; conversions x value gives revenue.

finalQuiz.q: A query has 5,000 impressions at position 14 and 25 clicks. The site's top-five queries average 4% CTR. What are the optimistic extra clicks?
According to Google, which canonical signal is weakest?
finalQuiz.explain: Google describes redirects and rel=canonical as strong signals and sitemap inclusion as a weak one.

finalQuiz.q: http://site.ng redirects to https://site.ng, which redirects to https://www.site.ng. What should be fixed?
options: Redirect every variant straight to https://www.site.ng in one hop
finalQuiz.explain: Redirect chains slow users and crawling; each variant should go to the final URL in a single permanent redirect.

finalQuiz.q: A brand has pages for Nigeria, Ghana and a general international page. Which hreflang set is correct?
options: en-NG, en-GH, x-default, on every version
en-NG on the Nigeria page only
finalQuiz.explain: Codes need a language plus optional ISO region, every version must list all versions including itself, and x-default marks the fallback.

finalQuiz.q: The free Screaming Frog SEO Spider is limited to how many URLs per crawl?
finalQuiz.explain: The free version crawls up to 500 URLs, enough for most small business sites.

finalQuiz.q: PageSpeed Insights shows good field data but a poor lab score. What does this usually mean?
options: Real visitors mostly have a good experience; the lab test is harsher
Core Web Vitals do not apply to the site
finalQuiz.explain: Field data reflects real Chrome users at the 75th percentile; lab data is one controlled test and is often stricter.

finalQuiz.q: Which finding should go first, regardless of its Impact x Confidence x Ease score?
options: A canonical tag on every page pointing to the old staging domain
finalQuiz.explain: Canonicals to a staging domain can push the live pages out of results. It is a critical blocker.

finalQuiz.q: CTR on changed pages rose from 2.0% to 2.6% while position stayed the same; unchanged comparison pages stayed flat. What is the best conclusion?
options: The change is likely responsible; report it as strong evidence
Nothing can be concluded from Search Console
The change guarantees permanent top rankings
finalQuiz.explain: Stable position and a flat comparison group make the change the likely cause, though it is evidence, not proof.

finalQuiz.q: What access should an SEO consultant normally request in Search Console?
options: Full user on the client's property
No access; work from screenshots only
finalQuiz.explain: Full user gives the data and tools needed while ownership and control stay with the client.

finalQuiz.q: A 3-month retainer is 12 hours a month at an illustrative 12,000 naira per hour. What is the total for the minimum term?
A prospective client asks you to guarantee position one within a month. What should you say?
options: Explain that no one can guarantee a number one ranking, and describe the indicator you will improve and report on
Promise position one but charge only if it happens
Offer to buy links to make it happen faster
finalQuiz.explain: Google states no one can guarantee a #1 ranking. Honest expectations and a clear measurement plan build trust; bought links break Google's spam policies.

capstone.title: SEO Audit and Client-Ready Report
capstone.brief: Audit one real website you have written permission to review, and produce a professional package: a documented technical and on-page audit with scored, prioritised recommendations; a client-facing report that translates findings into plain-language business impact; and a pricing proposal with a 90-day outreach plan aimed at one specific client type.
steps: Agree the audit with a real business owner, run a discovery call and get their written confirmation of a one-page brief.
Get full user access to Search Console (and Viewer access to analytics if available) and take a dated baseline snapshot.
Size the top three non-branded opportunities using the site's own CTR and conversion data, with conservative and optimistic cases.
Crawl the site, triage the Page indexing report and check speed, canonicals, redirects, titles and (if relevant) hreflang.
Check for critical blockers, then score every other finding with Impact x Confidence x Ease and group them into a 30/60/90-day roadmap.
Write at least three developer-ready tickets with acceptance criteria.
Write the client report: one-page executive summary, findings in plain language with evidence, roadmap, measurement plan and technical appendix.
Prepare a pricing proposal for implementing the roadmap and a 90-day outreach plan for your chosen niche, with funnel targets.
evidence: Signed or written confirmation of the brief and permission to audit
Dated baseline exports from Search Console and the crawl
Opportunity sizing sheet with formulas visible
Scored findings sheet with critical blockers marked
Client-ready report with a one-page executive summary
Pricing proposal with hours, rate, contingency, inclusions and exclusions
90-day outreach plan with weekly targets and checkpoints
